Q001718.stem: A startup needs encrypted connectivity from its office to a VPC this week, with about 200 Mbps of unpredictable traffic, while it evaluates Direct Connect over the next quarter. Which option fits, and what is its main limitation?

choices.text: Site-to-Site VPN; each tunnel tops out around 1.25 Gbps
VPC peering to the office network over the internet
A dedicated 10 Gbps Direct Connect port, which is always cheaper than VPN
A hosted Direct Connect connection, which encrypts traffic by default

Q001718.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Site-to-Site VPN is IPsec-encrypted, can be set up in minutes with no long-term commitment, and easily carries 200 Mbps. Its main limit is per-tunnel throughput (about 1.25 Gbps) over the variable internet path.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dedicated 10 Gbps DX: takes weeks to provision, and port hours are costly for 200 Mbps.
• Hosted DX: not encrypted by default, and provisioning takes time through a partner.
• VPC peering: connects VPCs only, not on-premises networks.

Key takeaway: fast, encrypted, low commitment → VPN; consistent high bandwidth → Direct Connect.

Q001737.stem: A company has Shield Advanced on an internet-facing ALB and wants automatic application-layer DDoS mitigation, with rules created and removed during attacks without manual work. What is required?

choices.text: Put the ALB behind CloudFront, since automatic L7 mitigation works only there
Associate a WAF web ACL with the ALB and enable automatic mitigation
Use a fixed target group without Auto Scaling
Disable AWS WAF, since Shield Advanced replaces its rule engine

Q001737.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced's automatic application layer mitigation places rules in a WAF web ACL associated with the protected resource. Without a web ACL on the ALB, it has nowhere to put mitigation rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront only: ALBs are supported when a web ACL is associated.
• Disabling WAF: removes the mechanism mitigation depends on.
• Fixed target group: unrelated to mitigation.

Key takeaway: Shield Advanced L7 auto-mitigation = rules inside your WAF web ACL.

Q001771.stem: A security team receives hundreds of GuardDuty findings daily in 30 accounts. It wants only findings with severity 7 or higher to page on-call immediately, and lower findings to go to a ticket queue. Which design fits?

choices.text: EventBridge rules with numeric severity filters routing to different targets
A CloudWatch metric filter on the GuardDuty console log
Configure GuardDuty in each account to generate only findings with severity 7 or higher
Security Hub's built-in paging for high findings

Q001771.explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty publishes findings to EventBridge. Numeric matching on detail.severity (for example, ≥7) routes high findings to a paging target and lower ones to a ticketing target. With a delegated administrator, findings arrive centrally.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only high findings: GuardDuty can't be limited this way; suppression rules archive, not route.
• Console log metric filter: there's no such log to filter.
• Security Hub paging: no built-in paging; it also emits to EventBridge.

Key takeaway: route findings by severity with EventBridge content filtering.

Q001774.stem: A security lead wants a dashboard view in Security Hub showing which 10 resources have the most failed high-severity findings across all accounts, updated automatically. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A security standard enabled for the organization
An automation rule that suppresses low-severity findings
A custom insight grouping filtered findings by resource ID
A custom action that sends findings to EventBridge

Q001774.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Insights are saved queries that group findings by an attribute. A custom insight filtered to failed high-severity findings and grouped by resource ID shows the most affected resources, updating as findings change.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom action: sends selected findings to EventBridge; not a view.
• Automation rule: modifies findings, such as suppressing them; not reporting.
• Standard: generates findings; doesn't aggregate them by resource.

Key takeaway: 'group findings by X' = insight.

Q001781.stem: A trail logs default events. During an incident, the team can see who changed a bucket policy but not who downloaded objects from the bucket. Why, and how is it fixed?

choices.text: Downloads are management events that expire after 24 hours
Object reads are logged only when S3 Versioning is enabled on the bucket
CloudTrail never logs S3 activity; use VPC Flow Logs
Object reads are data events; enable S3 data events (selector)

Q001781.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bucket policy changes are management (control plane) events, logged by default. Object-level reads (GetObject) are data events, logged only when enabled, preferably with advanced event selectors scoped to the relevant buckets to control cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 24-hour expiry: management events are kept 90 days in event history and indefinitely in a trail.
• Never logs S3: data events do exactly this.
• Versioning: unrelated to logging.

Key takeaway: control plane = management events; object or item operations = data events.

Q001801.stem: After a GuardDuty finding on an EC2 instance, an analyst needs to see, without writing queries, which IPs it talked to, which roles it used, and how its API activity compared with its normal baseline over the past weeks. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Macie
Amazon Inspector
AWS Config
Amazon Detective

Q001801.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Detective automatically builds behavior graphs from flow logs, CloudTrail, and GuardDuty findings, and presents entity profiles and baselines for investigation without manual queries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector: vulnerability management.
• Macie: sensitive data discovery.
• Config: resource configuration history, not behavioral activity.

Key takeaway: investigate who, what, and how unusual → Detective.

Q001803.stem: When GuardDuty reports a compromised instance, a company wants isolation, disk and memory capture, and evidence stored in a forensics account, repeatably and with no manual steps. Which approach fits?

choices.text: An Inspector rule that terminates the instance
A Config rule that rebuilds the instance from its AMI
The Automated Forensics Orchestrator for EC2 solution
Auto Scaling health checks replacing the instance

Q001803.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Automated Forensics Orchestrator uses EventBridge and Step Functions to isolate the instance, acquire disk and memory, and move evidence to a forensics account, triggered by security findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Termination: destroys volatile evidence.
• Rebuilding from an AMI: loses evidence and doesn't isolate.
• ASG replacement: terminates the compromised instance, losing evidence.

Key takeaway: preserve evidence before remediation; automate the steps.

Q001810.stem: During a ransomware drill, responders lost 40 minutes finding which role to assume, which forensics account to use, and who could approve isolation. What would MOST reduce this delay?

choices.text: Rely on responders searching AWS documentation during incidents
Enable more GuardDuty protection plans
Grant all responders AdministratorAccess in every account
Versioned runbooks with exact accounts, roles, and approvers

Q001810.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Runbooks list pre-approved steps, the exact account IDs, role ARNs, and decision owners, so responders act immediately and consistently. Tabletop exercises should keep them current.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Admin everywhere: expands attack surface and still lacks procedure.
• Searching docs: exactly what caused the delay.
• More detection: doesn't speed up response.

Key takeaway: speed comes from preparation: specific, tested runbooks.

Q001819.stem: An instance in a subnet with 20 other instances is suspected compromised. The team must cut off only this instance while keeping it running for forensics. Which control fits?

choices.text: Stop the instance and detach its volumes
Remove the subnet's route to the NAT gateway
Add deny rules for the instance's IP to the subnet's network ACL
Replace its security groups with an isolation security group

Q001819.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security groups apply per network interface, so changing only this instance's groups isolates it without affecting the other 20. Note that existing tracked connections may persist, so combine with other controls if needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NACL: affects every instance in the subnet.
• Route removal: also affects the whole subnet, and only outbound.
• Stopping: destroys memory evidence.

Key takeaway: instance-level isolation → security group swap.

Q001829.stem: A retailer expects DDoS attacks during a sale. It wants 24/7 expert help during attacks, proactive engagement when health checks fail, and credits for attack-driven scaling. Which subscription provides these?

choices.text: GuardDuty with Runtime Monitoring
Shield Advanced, with proactive engagement configured
AWS WAF Bot Control managed rules
Shield Standard, which is included for all customers

Q001829.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced adds access to the Shield Response Team, proactive engagement (SRT contacts you when associated health checks show impact during an event), and DDoS cost protection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shield Standard: automatic L3/L4 protection only.
• Bot Control: WAF rules for bots, not DDoS support.
• GuardDuty: threat detection.

Key takeaway: people + proactive contact + cost protection → Shield Advanced.

Q001832.stem: One web ACL must protect a CloudFront distribution and another an ALB in us-west-2. A team tried to create both in us-west-2 and couldn't associate one of them. Which setup is correct?

choices.text: Scope is chosen automatically by AWS WAF based on each resource's tags
Both with CLOUDFRONT scope, since the scopes are shared
CloudFront ACL: CLOUDFRONT scope (us-east-1); ALB ACL: REGIONAL in us-west-2
Both with REGIONAL scope in us-west-2

Q001832.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Web ACLs for CloudFront use the CLOUDFRONT (global) scope, managed in us-east-1. Web ACLs for ALB, API Gateway, and similar resources use REGIONAL scope in the resource's Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both REGIONAL: can't be associated with CloudFront.
• Both CLOUDFRONT: can't be associated with an ALB.
• Automatic scope: you choose it explicitly.

Key takeaway: CloudFront = global scope in us-east-1; everything else = the resource's Region.

Q001838.stem: A pentest shows an SSRF flaw could read instance role credentials. Containers on the host legitimately need IMDS. Which change blocks SSRF-style access while keeping container access working?

choices.text: Block 169.254.169.254 with a security group rule
Rotate the instance role credentials every 15 minutes with a scheduled Lambda
Disable IMDS entirely on all instances
Require IMDSv2; set hop limit 2 only where containers need it

Q001838.explanation:
Why this is correct:
IMDSv2 requires a PUT to get a session token, which typical SSRF can't perform. A hop limit of 2 lets containers behind a bridge reach IMDS; hosts without containers can keep hop limit 1.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable IMDS: breaks containers that need credentials.
• SG rule: security groups can't filter link-local metadata traffic.
• Faster rotation: stolen credentials still work until expiry.

Key takeaway: SSRF protection for IMDS → IMDSv2; tune hop limits for containers.

Q001843.stem: A new critical CVE is disclosed. Security must list every EC2 instance, ECR image, and Lambda function affected across 50 accounts within hours, prioritized by network exposure. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Config advanced queries on instance tags and installed software inventory
Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection
Amazon Inspector with an org delegated administrator
Amazon Macie automated discovery

Q001843.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inspector continuously scans EC2, ECR, and Lambda, automatically re-evaluates when new CVEs are published, and its findings can be filtered by CVE ID across the organization, with risk scores that factor in network reachability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty Malware: malware, not CVEs.
• Config queries: have no CVE data.
• Macie: sensitive data.

Key takeaway: 'which of our resources have CVE-X' → Inspector.

Q001846.stem: A compliance report requires missing patches to be known daily, but installation must happen only in Sunday maintenance windows. How should Patch Manager be configured?

choices.text: Install on every boot using EC2 user data
A daily Install operation, since Install also reports compliance
A daily Scan operation, with Install scheduled in a Sunday window
Scan only, since Install requires Session Manager

Q001846.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Scan checks instances against the patch baseline and reports compliance without changing anything. Install applies approved missing patches (and may reboot), so it belongs in the maintenance window.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily Install: patches and reboots outside the approved window.
• Install via Session Manager: Install runs through Run Command documents.
• User data: runs only at launch.

Key takeaway: Scan to report, Install to change.

Q001850.stem: An app server initiates HTTPS calls to an external API. Its SG allows all outbound traffic, and the subnet NACL allows outbound 443 and inbound 443 only. Calls time out. Why?

choices.text: The API must allow port 443 in its own NACL
The stateless NACL must allow inbound ephemeral ports for replies
The security group needs an inbound rule allowing replies from the API's IP range
NACLs don't apply to outbound-initiated traffic

Q001850.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Replies from the API come back to the server's ephemeral source port. Security groups track the connection, but NACLs are stateless, so inbound ephemeral ports (1024-65535) must be allowed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG inbound rule: stateful SGs allow return traffic automatically.
• NACLs apply to all traffic crossing the subnet.
• The API side: not within the customer's control, and not the cause here.

Key takeaway: with NACLs, think in both directions and remember ephemeral ports.

Q001860.stem: An admin updated a permission set, but users in some accounts still see old permissions, and in one account a local admin edited the AWSReservedSSO role directly. What is true?

choices.text: Local edits to the SSO role are the recommended way to customize access
Permission sets apply only to the management account
Permission sets are evaluated live by Identity Center, not IAM
Sets become IAM roles per account; reprovision to update or overwrite

Q001860.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Identity Center creates and manages an IAM role in each assigned account from the permission set. Updates reach accounts when the permission set is provisioned, and local edits to these managed roles are unsupported and can be overwritten.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Live evaluation: IAM evaluates the role in each account.
• Local edits: not a supported customization path.
• Management account only: permission sets apply to any assigned account.

Key takeaway: permission set → managed IAM role per account; reprovision after changes.

Q001864.stem: A SPA uses Cognito user pool hosted UI. The backend API must authorize requests, and the app must keep users signed in for 30 days without re-entering passwords. Which tokens should be used how?

choices.text: Refresh token sent on every API call as a bearer token
ID token as AWS credentials to call S3 and the API
Session token from STS returned directly by the user pool
Access token to call the API; refresh token for new tokens

Q001864.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cognito returns ID, access, and refresh tokens. APIs should authorize with the access token (scopes), the ID token describes the user to the app, and the refresh token gets new tokens without re-authentication for its configured lifetime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ID token as AWS credentials: it's a JWT, not AWS credentials; those come from identity pools.
• Refresh token on API calls: exposes a long-lived token and isn't meant for authorization.
• STS session tokens: not issued by user pools.

Key takeaway: API authorization → access token; identity → ID token; longevity → refresh token.

Q001873.stem: Administrators were phished via a fake AWS sign-in page that relayed TOTP codes in real time. Which MFA type would have prevented this?

choices.text: Hardware TOTP tokens kept in a safe and used only by administrators
SMS codes to registered phones
FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys bound to the real origin
Virtual TOTP apps with shorter 15-second codes

Q001873.explanation:
Why this is correct:
FIDO2/WebAuthn keys cryptographically bind the sign-in to the legitimate domain, so a relay site can't use the response. Any code a user can type (TOTP or SMS) can be relayed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shorter TOTP: still relayable in real time.
• SMS: relayable, and also vulnerable to SIM swap.
• Hardware TOTP: still produces relayable codes.

Key takeaway: phishing-resistant = origin-bound (FIDO2).

Q001875.stem: A role's identity policy allows s3:*, the bucket policy allows the role, and a permissions boundary allows s3:*, but an SCP denies s3:DeleteObject. What happens when the role deletes an object?

choices.text: Denied only if the bucket is in another account
Allowed: three policies allow it and only one denies
Allowed: resource policies override SCPs in the same account
Denied: an explicit Deny in any applicable policy wins

Q001875.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Policy evaluation checks for explicit denies across all applicable policy types first. Any explicit Deny, including from an SCP, ends the evaluation with deny, regardless of allows elsewhere.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Majority rules: IAM doesn't count votes.
• Resource policy overriding SCP: SCPs limit principals in member accounts regardless.
• Cross-account only: the SCP applies in the same account too.

Key takeaway: explicit Deny anywhere = denied.

Q001884.stem: A KMS key in Account A must be used by a Lambda role in Account B. Which policies must allow the call?

choices.text: A's key policy allowing B, and B's role identity policy
An SCP in Account A that grants Account B permission to use the key
Only the key policy in Account A
Only the role's identity policy in Account B

Q001884.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account access needs both sides: the resource-based policy (here, the key policy) must trust the external principal, and the principal's identity policy must allow the action on that key.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identity policy only: the key owner must also allow it.
• Key policy only: for cross-account calls, the caller's own policy must allow it too.
• SCPs: never grant permissions.

Key takeaway: cross-account = resource policy + identity policy.

Q001885.stem: A company has 200 projects and wants engineers to access only resources tagged with their own project, without writing a policy per project. Engineers sign in through an IdP that sends a project attribute. Which approach fits?

choices.text: One role per project with resource ARNs listed
One account per project
ABAC matching aws:PrincipalTag to aws:ResourceTag, with session tags
Resource policies on each resource listing every engineer's ARN

Q001885.explanation:
Why this is correct:
ABAC compares principal tags (from session tags passed by the IdP) with resource tags in a small set of policies, so new projects need only tags, not new policies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Role per project: 200 roles and policies to maintain.
• Resource policies with ARNs: unmanageable at scale.
• Account per project: heavy operational overhead.

Key takeaway: scale permissions with tags (ABAC).

Q001890.stem: A SaaS app needs rules like 'managers can approve expenses under $10,000 in their department', changed without redeploying code and evaluated consistently across services. Which fits?

choices.text: AWS WAF custom rules
Cognito user pool groups mapped to application roles
IAM policies for each end user
Amazon Verified Permissions with Cedar policies

Q001890.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Verified Permissions externalizes application authorization into Cedar policies, evaluated via the IsAuthorized API, with attribute-based conditions (amount, department) and no code redeploys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM per user: IAM governs AWS resources, not app decisions for end users.
• Groups only: too coarse for attribute conditions.
• WAF: filters requests, not business authorization.

Key takeaway: app-level fine-grained authz → Verified Permissions.

Q001902.stem: An ACM certificate for app.example.com was requested in eu-west-1 for a CloudFront distribution, but it doesn't appear in the distribution settings. What should be done?

choices.text: Attach it to an ALB origin in eu-west-1 instead
Request (or import) the certificate in us-east-1
Validate it again with email validation
Copy the certificate from eu-west-1 with the ACM API

Q001902.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront uses ACM certificates from us-east-1 only, regardless of where the origin or viewers are.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Copying: public ACM certificates can't be copied between Regions.
• ALB origin: secures the origin connection, not the viewer-facing domain on CloudFront.
• Revalidation: validation method isn't the problem.

Key takeaway: CloudFront certificates live in us-east-1.

Q001904.stem: Every new EBS volume in a Region must be encrypted with a specific customer managed key, including volumes created by services and by users who forget to choose encryption. Which setting fits?

choices.text: A tag policy requiring an Encrypted tag
An SCP denying CreateVolume unless encryption is requested
A Config rule that flags unencrypted volumes
EBS encryption by default with that CMK as the default key

Q001904.explanation:
Why this is correct:
EBS encryption by default is a per-Region account setting that encrypts all new volumes and snapshot copies automatically, and you can set the default KMS key to your CMK.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCP: blocks some calls rather than encrypting them, and can break services.
• Config rule: detective only.
• Tag policy: tags don't encrypt anything.

Key takeaway: encrypt everything automatically → encryption by default + default CMK.

Q001916.stem: The governance team must know which of 1,200 buckets across the org contain PII, updated continuously, at controlled cost, with findings routed to Security Hub. Which approach fits?

choices.text: GuardDuty S3 Protection
Macie automated discovery via a delegated admin, integrated with Security Hub
S3 Inventory reports
Daily full Macie classification jobs over every object in every bucket

Q001916.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie's automated sensitive data discovery samples objects across all buckets continuously for cost-effective coverage, and Macie can publish findings to Security Hub.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily full jobs: very costly at this scale.
• GuardDuty S3: detects access threats, not content.
• Inventory: lists objects; no classification.

Key takeaway: sensitive data in S3 → Macie; estate-wide at low cost → automated discovery.

Q001926.stem: Control Tower shows a guardrail that stops users from disabling CloudTrail and another that reports buckets without encryption. What are their types and mechanisms?

choices.text: Preventive via SCPs; detective via Config rules
Both proactive via CloudFormation hooks
Preventive via Config rules; detective via SCPs
Both detective via Config rules

Q001926.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Preventive controls block actions using SCPs (or RCPs). Detective controls report noncompliance using AWS Config rules. Proactive controls check resources before provisioning using CloudFormation hooks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both detective: the first one blocks actions.
• Reversed: SCPs block; Config detects.
• Proactive: applies to CloudFormation provisioning only.

Key takeaway: preventive = SCP, detective = Config, proactive = CFN hooks.

Q001947.stem: A compliance manager needs SOC 2 evidence (Config results, CloudTrail activity, and manual attestations) continuously collected, mapped to controls, and exported as an assessment report. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Config alone
AWS Audit Manager with a SOC 2 framework
AWS Artifact
AWS Security Hub with the SOC 2-aligned standards enabled

Q001947.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Audit Manager collects evidence from AWS sources and manual uploads, maps it to framework controls, and produces assessment reports.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Artifact: AWS's own compliance reports.
• Security Hub: findings and scores, not control-mapped evidence packages.
• Config: evaluations only.

Key takeaway: control-mapped audit evidence → Audit Manager.
